pages.ocr_text: Focus in the dual-self model
pages.summary:
This page presents a conceptual diagram illustrating the "dual-self model" using an elephant and rider metaphor. The model contrasts two self-systems: the long-term, patient planner (represented by the rider) and the short-term, impulsive doer (represented by the elephant). The text explains that the rider can understand the cumulative benefits of focus over many years, while the elephant gets bored with repetition and wants to move on to new experiences. The visual elements include labeled boxes for each self and a central illustration of the metaphor.

**Text Evidence:**
- The title is "Focus in the dual-self model"
- The rider represents the long-term, patient, planner, impartial spectator, deliberative, cold state
- The elephant represents the short-term, impulsive, doer, passions, affective/visceral, hot state
- The rider can understand the cumulative benefits of focus over many years
- The elephant gets bored with repetition and wants to move on to the next new experience

**Visual Evidence:**
<figure_summary>Figure 1: Dual-self model diagram - A central illustration of an elephant carrying a rider, with two colored boxes connected by lines. The blue box on the left lists attributes of the "Long-term" self (rider), and the red box on the bottom left lists attributes of the "Short-term" self (elephant).</figure_summary>

Focus v. variety in medical skills

Figure: Figure 4. Two trends for development of medical performance as a function of experience and instruction.
pages.summary:
This page presents Figure 4, a line graph illustrating two contrasting trends in medical performance development. The solid line shows that performance for specialists increases with instruction and experience, peaking at the "Specialist" level after training as a "Student" and "Resident." In contrast, the dashed line shows that general practitioners' performance peaks early (within 0-9 years) and then declines over time (10-20 years, Over 20 years). The figure is titled "Two trends for development of medical performance as a function of experience and instruction" and is sourced from research by Butterworth and Reppert (1960) and Ericsson (2004).

**Text Evidence:**
- The title is "Focus v. variety in medical skills."
- The figure caption states it shows "Two trends for development of medical performance as a function of experience and instruction."
- The graph compares the performance trajectory of Specialists versus General Practitioners.
- The source is cited as Butterworth, J. (NYU), Reppert, E. (NYU), 1960, and Ericsson, K. A. (Florida State U.), 2004.

**Visual Evidence:**

- The significant psychological subscale was: 4. I remain positive and enthusiastic during competition, no matter how badly things are going.
